The Globe fish (Tetraodon lineatus) inhabits the lower reaches of the Niger and Volta river systems, where it occupies both floodplain lagoons and main channel areas with submerged vegetation. Field surveys estimating age structure through otolith micro-increment analysis have documented that under a stable thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum recorded longevity extends to approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years], though most individuals in exploited populations are captured before reaching this upper limit. The species exhibits a relatively slow growth trajectory compared to many sympatric teleosts, a pattern frequently linked to its heavily armoured morphology and benthic foraging habits centred on molluscs and crustaceans. Female and male growth trajectories appear essentially isometric across the size range, and histological examination of gonadal material indicates that reproductive activity commences at a comparatively modest size. These demographic traits place Tetraodon lineatus among the longer-lived pufferfishes within its phylogenetic clade, with a life-history strategy apparently oriented toward adult survival rather than high fecundity, consistent with the constraints imposed by its specialised durophagous diet.

Reproductive maturation in this species has been assessed through macroscopic staging of gonadal development in specimens collected during seasonal flood pulses. The total length at which 50% of individuals display active gametogenesis is 18.2 cm [Lp = 18.2 cm], indicating that puberty is attained at a size considerably smaller than the maximum recorded for the species. This threshold appears consistent across the geographic range of the species, with no detectable difference between populations from the Niger and Volta basins. Histological sections reveal that vitellogenic oocytes and spermatocytes are already present in fish approaching this length, confirming that the onset of gonadal recrudescence occurs during the late juvenile phase. The relatively early maturation likely represents an adaptation to unpredictable flood regimes, allowing some reproductive output before the risk of being stranded in isolated pools during the dry season. Comparative data from other Tetraodon species indicate that this maturation length is intermediate, reflecting a balance between the advantages of early reproduction and the energetic demands of continued somatic growth.

Once individuals attain puberty, they continue to invest heavily in body size increase, and adult specimens can eventually reach a substantial ultimate total length of 43 cm [Li = 43 cm], though individuals exceeding 40 cm are uncommon in most survey catches. This maximum length corresponds to a substantial adult body mass, with the heaviest individuals recorded in floodplain habitats attaining an ultimate wet weight of 1300 grams [Wwi = 1300 grams]. The strong positive allometry between length and mass in this species reflects the development of a deep, laterally compressed body and a large, powerful jaw apparatus required for crushing hard-shelled prey. Growth increments measured from recaptured marked individuals suggest that the asymptotic size is approached after several years of sustained feeding on productive floodplain invertebrates. The size dimorphism between sexes is negligible, and both males and females appear to follow similar growth trajectories until senescence. Attaining such a large body size likely confers fitness advantages, including reduced predation risk from gape-limited piscivores and the ability to exploit larger, more nutritionally rewarding prey items unavailable to smaller congeners.

The earliest life stages of Tetraodon lineatus are poorly documented in the wild, but extrapolation from egg diameters measured in related pufferfish species provides a reasonable approximation of neonatal mass. Based on the average egg diameter of Sphoeroides maculatus, the estimated wet weight at birth is approximately 0.00036 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00036 grams], a value typical of the small, pelagic eggs produced by many tetraodontiform fishes following external fertilisation. The yolk-sac larva that emerges at eclosion is lecithotrophic for a brief period, relying entirely on endogenous reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. Observations under captive rearing conditions indicate that the yolk absorption stage lasts only a few days, after which the prolarva must begin capturing small zooplankton. The minute size at hatching renders the early larvae highly vulnerable to starvation and planktivorous predators, imposing a selective bottleneck that likely regulates recruitment strength in natural populations. This high mortality risk during the early larval phase is a common feature among marine and freshwater teleosts that produce numerous, small offspring.

Under stable thermal conditions of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) of actively spawning females reaches a mean value of 6.5% [GSI = 6.5%]. This index, derived from gravid females collected during the peak of the flood season, suggests that ovarian mass constitutes approximately 6.5% of total body weight at spawning. Histological analysis of these ovaries reveals a batch-spawning pattern, with oocytes at multiple developmental stages present simultaneously, indicating that individual females may release several clutches over the course of a single reproductive season. The energetic cost of repeated spawning events is partially offset by the abundant prey availability characteristic of flooded riparian zones.
